name: Faces of Poverty: Two Typical Cases

scenes.animation: Zippy happily munches a samosa outside a railway station. His eyes move to a child in torn clothes watching him from a distance. Zippy stops chewing, breaks the samosa in half, and the camera slowly pulls back to show many such faces across the station.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I never noticed how many people around us are struggling.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In fact, every fourth person in India is poor. That is roughly two hundred and seventy million, or twenty-seven crore people, in 2011-12.

scenes.animation: An urban case file opens: 'Ram Saran, 33, daily-wage labourer in a wheat flour mill near Ranchi, Jharkhand'. Icons fill in: a one-room rented shack in a crowded basti, a family of six, dal and rice twice a day, children not in school, only two pairs of clothes each.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Meet Ram Saran. He is thirty-three and works as a daily-wage labourer in a wheat flour mill near Ranchi in Jharkhand. He finds work only now and then.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: His family of six lives in a one-room rented house in a crowded basti. They manage a meagre meal of dal and rice twice a day. None of the children go to school, and the younger ones are undernourished.

scenes.animation: A rural case file opens: 'Lakha Singh, small village near Meerut, Uttar Pradesh'. Icons: a kuchha hut, odd jobs for big farmers, wages sometimes paid in wheat or dal, a family of eight, a father who died of TB for lack of medicine, a school he never attended.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now meet Lakha Singh, from a small village near Meerut in Uttar Pradesh. His family owns no land, so they do odd jobs for big farmers, sometimes paid only in wheat or dal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: His family of eight cannot always manage two square meals a day. His father died of TB for lack of medication. Lakha never went to school and started earning when he was ten.

scenes.animation: A word cloud forms from both case files: 'Landlessness', 'Unemployment', 'Size of families', 'Illiteracy', 'Poor health', 'Child labour', 'Helplessness'. The word 'Helplessness' pulses largest.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: These cases show that poverty means hunger and lack of shelter. It means parents cannot send children to school and sick people cannot afford treatment.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It means lack of clean water, sanitation and a regular job. Above all, it means living with a sense of helplessness.

scenes.animation: Two new lenses slide over the scene. Lens 1, 'Social exclusion': a poor family is kept outside a fence while others enjoy facilities. Lens 2, 'Vulnerability': a flood wave approaches and some houses have no safety net. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Social scientists look at poverty through more indicators. Social exclusion is a process through which individuals or groups are excluded from facilities, benefits and opportunities that others enjoy. The caste system is a typical example.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Vulnerability describes the greater probability of certain communities or individuals becoming, or remaining, poor in the coming years, for example when a flood strikes or jobs disappear.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: define social exclusion and vulnerability in your own words, with one example each.

scenes.animation: Recap board with two case-file icons: '1. Every fourth Indian is poor: about 270 million in 2011-12', '2. Poverty = hunger, no shelter, no schooling, no healthcare, helplessness', '3. Social exclusion and vulnerability'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: every fourth person in India is poor.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Ram Saran and Lakha Singh show that poverty affects food, shelter, schooling, health and dignity.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: social exclusion and vulnerability help us see poverty more fully.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Poverty isn't just about money. Got it.

name: The Poverty Line and Poverty Estimates

scenes.animation: A long horizontal rope is stretched across a village and a city, labelled 'Poverty line'. Zippy walks on it like a tightrope walker, wobbling. People below it hold empty plates.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Is the poverty line a real line? Can I walk on it?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It's an imaginary line. A person is considered poor if his or her income or consumption falls below a minimum level needed to meet basic needs.

scenes.animation: A plate fills with cereals, pulses, vegetables, milk, oil and sugar. Calorie meters appear: 'Rural: 2400 calories per person per day' with a farmer ploughing, and 'Urban: 2100 calories per person per day' with an office worker.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In India, the poverty line considers minimum needs for food, clothing, footwear, fuel and light, education and medical care.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The food requirement is based on calories. The accepted average is two thousand four hundred calories per person per day in rural areas and two thousand one hundred in urban areas.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Rural people do more physical work, so their requirement is higher.

scenes.animation: A money meter shows '2011-12 poverty line: ₹816 per person per month (rural), ₹1000 (urban)'. It multiplies: 'Family of five: about ₹4,080 (rural), ₹5,000 (urban)'. A label reads 'Estimated every five years through NSSO surveys'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For 2011-12, the poverty line was fixed at eight hundred and sixteen rupees per person per month in rural areas and one thousand rupees in urban areas.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Urban needs are lower in calories, but many essential products cost more in cities. The poverty line is estimated periodically, normally every five years, through sample surveys by the National Sample Survey Organisation.

scenes.animation: A data table builds row by row with columns 'Year | Poverty ratio % (Rural, Urban, Total) | Number of poor, millions': '1993-94: 50.1, 31.8, about 45 | 403.7', '2004-05: 41.8, 25.7, 37.2 | 407.1', '2011-12: 25.7, 13.7, 21.9 | 269.3'. A line graph drops alongside.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Poverty ratios in India fell substantially, from about forty-five per cent in 1993-94 to 37.2 per cent in 2004-05. By 2011-12, it came down to about 21.9 per cent.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The number of poor fell from 407.1 million in 2004-05 to 269.3 million in 2011-12.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Wait, the ratio fell between 1993 and 2004, but the number of poor went up slightly?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes, because the population grew. That's why we study both the ratio and the number.

scenes.animation: A globe spins with a single ruler labelled 'World Bank: uniform standard for comparing countries'. Beside it, a car shown in the USA with the note 'Different countries, different poverty lines'. An 'EXAM TIP' card flips over.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Each country uses a poverty line suited to its level of development. To compare developing countries, international organisations like the World Bank use a uniform standard.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: the calorie norms of 2400 and 2100, and the rupee figures of 816 and 1000, are frequently asked. Write rural and urban correctly.

scenes.animation: Recap board: '1. Poverty line: minimum level for basic needs; 2400 rural, 2100 urban calories', '2. 2011-12: ₹816 rural, ₹1000 urban per person per month', '3. Poverty ratio: about 45% (1993-94) → 21.9% (2011-12)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the poverty line is based on minimum needs, with calorie norms of 2400 in rural and 2100 in urban areas.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: in 2011-12, it was eight hundred and sixteen rupees for rural and one thousand for urban areas per month.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the poverty ratio fell from about forty-five per cent to 21.9 per cent.

name: Vulnerable Groups, Inter-State Disparities and Global Poverty

scenes.animation: A family sits down to eat. The father and son get full plates; the mother, grandmother and little daughter get smaller portions. Zippy frowns and pushes his own plate toward the girl.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why is the girl getting the smallest plate?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because poverty doesn't hit everyone equally, not even within one family.

scenes.animation: A bar chart builds: most vulnerable groups labelled 'Scheduled Caste households', 'Scheduled Tribe households', 'Rural agricultural labour households', 'Urban casual labour households'. Inside a family, icons for 'Women', 'Children, especially the girl child', 'Old people' are marked 'Poorest of the poor'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The social groups most vulnerable to poverty are scheduled caste and scheduled tribe households. Among economic groups, the most vulnerable are rural agricultural labour households and urban casual labour households.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Within poor families, women, elderly people and female infants are often denied equal access to resources. So women, children, especially the girl child, and old people are the poorest of the poor.

scenes.animation: A map of India is shaded by poverty. 'Bihar' and 'Odisha' glow darkest, labelled 'Two poorest states'. Other states light up with reasons: 'Punjab and Haryana: high agricultural growth', 'Kerala: human resource development', 'West Bengal: land reforms', 'Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu: public distribution of food grains'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The proportion of poor people is not the same in every state. Bihar and Odisha continue to be the two poorest states.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Other states reduced poverty in different ways. Punjab and Haryana used high agricultural growth. Kerala focused on human resource development. In West Bengal, land reform measures helped.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, public distribution of food grains could have been responsible for the improvement.

scenes.animation: A world map. China and Southeast Asia glow green with arrows labelled 'Rapid economic growth + investment in human resource development'. South Asia shows a slower decline. Sub-Saharan Africa glows red: 'Poverty declined much less'. Russia shows a small warning: 'Poverty resurfaced'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Globally, the proportion of people living in extreme poverty has fallen. But there are great regional differences.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Poverty declined substantially in China and Southeast Asian countries, due to rapid economic growth and massive investments in human resource development. In South Asia, the decline has not been as rapid.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sub-Saharan Africa remains a major concern, and poverty has resurfaced in some former socialist countries like Russia.

scenes.animation: A matching board: states on the left, reasons on the right, lines connecting them. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Punjab, farming. Kerala, people. West Bengal, land. Easy!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. Exam tip: the state-and-reason match is a favourite three-mark question.

scenes.animation: Recap board: '1. Most vulnerable: SC and ST households, rural agricultural labour, urban casual labour', '2. Bihar and Odisha poorest; Punjab, Kerala, West Bengal succeeded', '3. China fell fast; Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia slower'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: SC and ST households and rural and urban labour households are most vulnerable, and women, children and the elderly suffer most.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: poverty varies across states, with Bihar and Odisha the poorest.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: globally, China and Southeast Asia reduced poverty fastest.

name: Causes of Poverty and Anti-Poverty Measures

scenes.animation: A spinning wheel labelled 'Cycle of poverty' traps a small farmer: 'Low income' → 'Borrow for seeds and fertiliser' → 'Cannot repay' → 'Debt' → 'Low income'. Zippy tries to jump in and stop the wheel.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: How do people get stuck in this loop?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Let's look at the causes. Then we'll see how the government tries to break the cycle.

scenes.animation: A cause list builds with icons: 'Colonial rule: handicrafts ruined, textiles discouraged', 'Low growth + high population growth', 'Unequal distribution of land; land reforms not implemented properly', 'Social obligations and religious ceremonies', 'Indebtedness'. Small slums form on the edges of a city.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One historical reason is the low level of economic development under British rule. Colonial policies ruined traditional handicrafts and discouraged industries like textiles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Low growth combined with a high population growth rate kept per capita income low. Unable to find proper jobs in cities, many people became rickshaw pullers, vendors or construction workers and lived in slums.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Unequal distribution of land, poorly implemented land reforms, spending on social ceremonies, and indebtedness also cause poverty.

scenes.animation: A two-plank bridge crosses a river of poverty. Plank 1: 'Promotion of economic growth'. Plank 2: 'Targeted anti-poverty programmes'. A growth meter rises from 'About 3.5% in the 1970s' to 'About 6% in the 1980s and 1990s'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The government's anti-poverty strategy rests on two planks: promotion of economic growth, and targeted anti-poverty programmes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Growth jumped from an average of about three and a half per cent a year in the 1970s to about six per cent in the 1980s and 1990s, helping to reduce poverty.

scenes.animation: An animated timeline builds scheme by scheme: '1993: PMRY, self-employment for educated unemployed youth', '1995: REGP, self-employment in rural areas and small towns', '1999: SGSY, self-help groups, bank credit and subsidy', '2000: PMGY, basic services', '2005: MGNREGA, 100 days of wage employment, one-third jobs for women'. An 'Antyodaya Anna Yojana' badge sits at the end.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, aims to provide one hundred days of wage employment to every rural household. One-third of the proposed jobs are reserved for women.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Prime Minister Rozgar Yojana, started in 1993, creates self-employment for educated unemployed youth. The Rural Employment Generation Programme came in 1995. Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana, in 1999, organises poor families into self-help groups.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana, launched in 2000, gives states extra help for basic services. Antyodaya Anna Yojana is another important scheme.

scenes.animation: A mixed report card reads 'Results: mixed'. Red notes: 'Improper implementation', 'Wrong targeting', 'Overlapping schemes'. A 'BOARD TIP' card flips over with 'MGNREGA 2005: 100 days' highlighted.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The results have been mixed, mainly due to lack of proper implementation and right targeting, and overlapping schemes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: match each scheme to its year and aim. MGNREGA, 2005, one hundred days, is asked almost every year.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a broken-wheel icon: '1. Causes: colonial legacy, low growth, population, unequal land, debt', '2. Strategy: economic growth + targeted programmes', '3. MGNREGA 2005, PMRY 1993, REGP 1995, SGSY 1999, PMGY 2000'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: poverty has historical, economic and social causes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: India fights poverty through economic growth and targeted programmes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: MGNREGA guarantees one hundred days of work, alongside schemes like PMRY, REGP, SGSY and PMGY.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Time to break that wheel for good.
